doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

title: Growing up near Los Angeles and wanting New York
summary: Born in Ventura, she heard what was left of the LA jazz scene as a teen and always wanted New York; her parents warmed once she was on the radio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Was Los Angeles — that’s where you’re from, correct?
Um hum. Actually born in Ventura.
Was it a good musical atmosphere to grow up in?
Well it had been. It was before I was there. And a little bit was still left. There was a lot of jazz there when I was too young to —

Yeah. There was a lot. But there was a little bit left by the time I was fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, and I got out to hear that. I heard Art Blakey, I heard Johnny Griffin, and of course I heard Coltrane and I heard a lot of things, McCoy Tyner. It wasn’t like New York. And I always had a feeling that I wanted to be in New York, since I was six years

old I was drawing — and I’ve never heard or seen anything — but I was drawing these apartment buildings with little mice sticking out of them for people, like a lot of people in every window. It was very funny.
How did your parents feel about your — the direction you seemed to be embracing in music?

Well they didn’t seem to think too much about it until they started hearing me on the radio and then they began to get a bit proud about it, when their friends said, “Oh I heard your daughter on the radio.” They liked that.
